clue.text: I act dumb and act tight-lipped

indicators.note: dumb here is taken as stupid or confused, so the two words I act are jumbled

parts.note: an act on stage is a turn, a short performance

explanation.surface: Someone told to play mute and keep their mouth shut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dumb' looks like the silence of the definition, but it signals the anagram: I ACT becomes TACI, and a variety act is a TURN.
explanation.definitionFit: Taciturn describes someone reserved who says very little, a close synonym for keeping one's lips sealed.

clue.text: Small, neat boat

parts.note: S is the usual abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
neat is an old word for cattle, so a single one is a cow

explanation.surface: A tidy little vessel is being admired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'neat' looks like an adjective for tidy, but it is the archaic noun for cattle, as in neat's-foot oil.
explanation.definitionFit: A scow is a flat-bottomed boat used for carrying cargo such as sand or gravel.

clue.text: Engineers meeting over a meal

parts.note: RE stands for the Royal Engineers, a British Army corps
over as in finished or gone by means past

explanation.surface: Engineers hold a conference across lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: RE is the Royal Engineers, the British Army's engineering corps; 'over' in the sense of done with gives PAST.
explanation.definitionFit: A repast is a formal or literary word for a meal or feast.

clue.text: Guys with candles in the hills

parts.note: guys are men
dips are candles made by dipping a wick repeatedly in tallow

explanation.surface: Men carrying candles walk up into the hills.
explanation.walkthrough: The MENDIPS are a range of limestone hills in Somerset, south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mendips, or Mendip Hills, are a named range of uplands south of Bristol.

clue.text: Veg for a film producer

definitions.meaning: veg is short for vegetables; this is a green one with florets
Albert 'Cubby' ... produced the James Bond films

explanation.surface: A vegetable intended for someone in the movie business.
explanation.definitionFit: The green vegetable shares its name with Cubby Broccoli, the producer behind the Bond film series.

clue.text: Omar, crazy about end of Rubaiyat, beginning to dine with Fitzgerald on sausage

indicators.note: about means the jumbled name goes round the next piece
crazy says the letters of Omar are thrown into disorder
end of picks the final letter of Rubaiyat
beginning to picks the opening letter of dine

parts.note: Ella Fitzgerald was the American jazz singer

explanation.surface: Omar Khayyam, maddened by the Rubaiyat's close, dines with the translator Fitzgerald on sausage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crazy' turns OMAR into MORA, which goes 'about' T (end of Rubaiyat) to make MORTA; D starts dine; Fitzgerald is not the Rubaiyat's translator here but singer ELLA.
explanation.definitionFit: Mortadella is a large Italian sausage of finely ground pork from Bologna.

clue.text: Slowly incorporating a building extension?

indicators.note: incorporating means taking a piece in as part of the whole

parts.note: lento is the musical direction for slowly

explanation.surface: An extension going up at a snail's pace.
explanation.walkthrough: LENTO is the Italian musical marking for a slow tempo; 'incorporating' puts A inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A lean-to is a shed or annexe whose roof rests against an existing wall, a simple addition to a building.

clue.text: An aristocrat abroad? Search me!

indicators.note: abroad can mean astray or widely scattered, so the letters are sent all over

explanation.surface: Someone asked about a foreign nobleman shrugs and says they have no idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abroad' also fits the picture of a foreign title, but it signals the anagram of SEARCH ME; 'Search me!' poses as an exclamation of ignorance.
explanation.definitionFit: A marchese is an Italian nobleman ranking as a marquis, a member of the aristocracy.

clue.text: A little winter honeysuckle flower

indicators.note: A little says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A sprig of honeysuckle that blooms in winter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower' reads as a bloom, but in crosswords it is often something that flows: a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A flower in crossword terms is a river, something that flows, and the Rhone flows through Switzerland and France.

clue.text: See six points

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals
E and W are the compass points east and west

explanation.surface: An instruction to look at six marks.
explanation.definitionFit: To view something is to look at or see it, a straightforward verb synonym.

clue.text: Police coming back, going in, going down, giving up

indicators.note: going in says the police piece is placed inside the next word

parts.note: going down in the sense of subsiding or lessening means abating

indicators.note: coming back means the letters for police are read in reverse

parts.note: CID is the Criminal Investigation Department of British police

explanation.surface: A breathless chain of police movements ending in surrender.
explanation.walkthrough: CID, the British police detective branch, 'coming back' gives DIC, which is 'going in' ABATING (going down, as a storm does).
explanation.definitionFit: Abdicating means renouncing a throne or responsibility, a form of giving it up.

clue.text: Not in place for kickoff

parts.note: not in, as of a batsman dismissed or someone away, is out
to place something is to set it down

explanation.surface: A player out of position when the match begins.
explanation.definitionFit: The outset is the start or beginning of something, as a kickoff starts a match.

clue.text: Draw cover for book for a fellow

indicators.note: cover means the first word wraps round the letter for book

parts.note: a stalemate is a deadlock or draw, especially in chess

explanation.surface: Someone sketching the jacket design for a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw' and 'cover' suggest artwork, but a draw is a STALEMATE, which 'cover's B.
explanation.definitionFit: A stablemate is a horse from the same stable, and by extension a colleague or companion from the same organisation.

clue.text: Courtesy title given to upstanding political theorist

indicators.note: given to means the title is attached to the end of the other piece

parts.note: upstanding as in standing out or raised up means proud
Hon, short for Honourable, is a courtesy title for children of peers

explanation.surface: An honorary title being conferred on a respectable thinker.
explanation.walkthrough: HON (the Honourable) is the British courtesy title for a peer's younger children; 'upstanding' is PROUD in the sense of projecting, as a nail stands proud.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon was a French anarchist thinker who wrote that property is theft.

clue.text: Soldiers ignoring railway station at first — babes in arms, perhaps

indicators.note: ignoring means leaving the railway letters out

parts.note: infantry are foot soldiers

indicators.note: at first picks the opening letter of station

explanation.surface: Troops passing by a station, holding babies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'babes in arms' plays on soldiers carrying arms, but it means infants still carried; INFANTRY 'ignoring' RY leaves INFANT, plus S.
explanation.definitionFit: Babes in arms are babies too young to walk, examples of very young children, hence the 'perhaps'.

clue.text: According to hearsay, "Endeavour" and many old ships

indicators.note: according to hearsay says the words are judged by how they sound when spoken

parts.note: to endeavour is to try, and many is reams, as in reams of paper; said together the two words are heard

explanation.surface: Rumour has it that Captain Cook's Endeavour was one of a fleet of antique vessels.
explanation.walkthrough: Endeavour suggests Cook's ship, but it is the verb TRY; said together with REAMS it sounds like the ancient galleys.
explanation.definitionFit: Triremes were ancient Greek and Roman war galleys with three banks of oars.

clue.text: Prince's sound boosters?

indicators.note: sound says a word for prince's is said out loud

parts.note: Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, so belonging to him is Philip's

explanation.surface: Asking whether a prince's audio gear amplifies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prince's' points to Prince Philip, the late Duke of Edinburgh; the Philips brand of electronics adds to the sound-equipment picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A fillip is a stimulus or boost, something that gives a lift, so fillips are boosters.

clue.text: Former vicar in religious environment

indicators.note: environment means the surrounding word encloses the clergyman

parts.note: pious means devoutly religious
Rev, short for Reverend, is the title of a vicar

explanation.surface: An ex-vicar still living among the devout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in religious environment' says the devout word surrounds the clergyman's title; 'Former' poses as a past-tense hint but is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Previous means earlier or prior, synonymous with former, as in a former or previous owner.

clue.text: The only bird of its kind in Arizona

definitions.text: The only bird of its kind
definitions.meaning: the mythical bird said to exist singly and rise from its own ashes

explanation.surface: A unique bird found in the American Southwest.
explanation.definitionFit: The phoenix is the legendary bird of which only one exists at a time; Phoenix is also Arizona's state capital.

clue.text: Almost cold food — typical of 15

indicators.note: almost means the word is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: chill is coldness
a dish is a prepared item of food

explanation.surface: A nearly cold meal like the ones toddlers leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 15 refers to the answer at 15-across, INFANTS; CHILL 'almost' drops its last L to give CHIL.
explanation.definitionFit: Childish means characteristic of young children, so it describes behaviour typical of infants.

clue.text: One who wrote odes in a church or a cemetery

indicators.note: in says the answer lies within the run of words that follow

explanation.surface: A poet whose odes were composed in a churchyard.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters bridge 'church', 'or', 'a' and 'cemetery'; the churchyard setting suggests Gray's Elegy, a false trail.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman poet Horace is famous for his four books of Odes.

clue.text: Journey in the heart of Austria accompanied by composer

indicators.note: the heart of picks the central letter of Austria

parts.note: Maurice Ravel was the French composer of Bolero

explanation.surface: A trip into central Austria in a composer's company.
explanation.walkthrough: AUSTRIA has seven letters, so its heart is the single T.
explanation.definitionFit: To travel is to journey; as nouns both mean a trip from place to place.

clue.text: Drink that is initially all there

indicators.note: initially picks the opening letter of the word that

parts.note: someone all there is mentally sound, or sane

explanation.surface: A drink that, at first, seems perfectly fine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that is' looks like the phrase i.e., but only 'that' is cut to its first letter; IS stands as written.
explanation.definitionFit: A tisane is a herbal tea, an infusion of leaves or flowers drunk as a beverage.

clue.text: Musicians with T Rex starting to upset REM members

indicators.note: starting picks the opening letter of Rex
members, read as the parts of a body regrouped, says the band's letters and upset are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as part of the pool
taken as written as part of the pool

explanation.surface: Two rock bands clash, with T Rex setting out to rile REM's line-up.
explanation.walkthrough: T plus R (Rex's start) then the letters of UPSET and REM rearranged give UMPETERS; the anagram signal is loose, and 'upset' poses as the indicator though its letters are fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Trumpeters are players of the trumpet, so they are musicians.

clue.text: Slice of bread found on island — food that's attractively presented

indicators.note: slice of takes just a small piece, the first letter, of bread

parts.note: an ait or eyot is a small river island, especially on the Thames

explanation.surface: A slice of bread turns up on an island as a tempting snack.
explanation.walkthrough: An AIT is a small island in a river, a word mostly heard in Britain for the islets of the Thames.
explanation.definitionFit: Bait is food set out to lure fish or animals, so it is presented to attract them.

clue.text: Cuckoo is in

definitions.meaning: cuckoo is slang for crazy or mad
a cricketer who is in, at the crease

explanation.surface: A cuckoo has arrived.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the side that is in is batting; a single batsman who is in bats.
explanation.definitionFit: Bats is slang for crazy, as in 'gone bats', and in cricket a player who is in bats.

clue.text: Reminder about pair of tights for attractive girl

indicators.note: about means the reminder word goes round the other piece

parts.note: a cue is a prompt or reminder, as given to an actor

indicators.note: pair of picks the first two letters of tights

explanation.surface: Someone leaves a note about a pair of tights for a pretty girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pair of tights' looks like hosiery, but it only takes the first two letters, TI.
explanation.definitionFit: Cutie is informal for an attractive or charming person, here a pretty girl.

clue.text: Dress suiting a saint

indicators.note: dress in the sense of arranging or setting in order, as in dressing ranks, signals rearrangement

explanation.surface: A garment that would suit a holy figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dress' poses as a noun for a garment, but it is a verb meaning arrange; St Ignatius Loyola founded the Jesuits.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignatius is the name of saints such as Ignatius Loyola and Ignatius of Antioch.
